Its most recognizable feature is the traditional reed boats known as caballitos de totora. The beach, ocean surf and fishing traditions give this place its distinctive character.

Visitors stroll along Huanchaco's waterfront and discover life in the settlement. A stop here complements a visit to Chan Chan: after exploring ancient adobe buildings, the route reaches the ocean and the living culture of the coast. The sight of the boats, the sea air and the open coastal landscape make the walk memorable.

Huaquechula is known for the family altars created in memory of loved ones who have died. They are decorated with flowers, candles and photographs. Favorite foods and personal belongings of those remembered are also part of the arrangements, so every altar tells a particular family's story.

A visit reveals the local traditions of the Day of the Dead. Here, the celebration is especially visible inside homes and in family customs, complementing the public events held in larger cities. Huaquechula is often visited alongside Cholula and Puebla, offering a chance to experience archaeological sites, colonial architecture and the region's living traditions.

Humahuaca is particularly known for the atmosphere of an old Andean settlement. Narrow cobbled streets, low houses made of adobe and stone, small squares, craft shops and traditional markets give the town its distinctive appearance. The connection with the region's ancient cultures remains tangible, while local festivals, music and folk crafts preserve traditions that go back centuries.

The town's main landmark is the Monument to the Heroes of Independence, which rises on a mountainside and commemorates the struggle for independence of the peoples of northern Argentina. From here, there are panoramic views over the town and the surrounding valley.

The central square plays a special part in Humahuaca's daily life. Nearby stand a historic church and the town hall. At certain times of day, a mechanical figure of Saint Francis appears on the town hall's façade, an unusual local tradition.

Yet it is the Quebrada de Humahuaca itself that leaves the strongest impression: a valley of extraordinary multicolored mountains shaped over millions of years. In sunlight, the reds, oranges, purples and golds of the rocks become especially vivid, creating a striking natural panorama.

Humahuaca is also an important center of Andean culture. Visitors can sample the traditional cuisine of northern Argentina, buy work by local artisans and experience the region's particular pace of life, where ancient customs continue alongside modern culture.

Humahuaca offers a journey into the heart of Andean Argentina, where history, long-standing traditions and extraordinary mountain scenery come together in a vivid image of northern Patagonia.

The name Iberá comes from the Guaraní language and means "shining waters," a fitting and poetic description of this landscape. In the sunlight, the surfaces of its many lagoons shimmer with silver and gold, reflecting the sky, reeds and surrounding vegetation.

Iberá is particularly renowned for its abundant wildlife. On boat outings or wetland safaris, visitors may see capybaras, caimans, marsh deer and monkeys, while dozens of bird species inhabit the skies above the water and vegetation. The region is also an important center for restoring populations of rare animals, including jaguars and giant otters.

One of the best ways to explore Iberá is by boat through the lagoons and waterways. Traveling on the water makes it possible to approach animals without disturbing their natural behavior, while experienced local guides help spot birds and marsh inhabitants that an untrained visitor might overlook.

Beyond boat excursions, walking trails, horseback rides and birdwatching are popular here. Sunrise and sunset are particularly memorable, when only birdsong breaks the wetland silence and the vast stretches of water reflect the sky.

Iberá is a place for travelers who want to discover a different Argentina: beyond mountains, glaciers and vineyards lies a living, humid and almost untouched natural world.

Iberá is a world of water and wildlife, where lagoons, reeds and green islands offer a genuine sense of closeness to South America's nature.
